1.summary: Told to preach against Nineveh, Jonah sails the other way; God sends a storm, the pagan sailors pray and finally throw Jonah overboard, and a great fish swallows him.
1.lookfor: Count how often Jonah goes down, notice how the sailors behave compared with the prophet, and watch the word great.

names.name: Jonah
names.gloss: A prophet from Gath Hepher in Galilee under Jeroboam II; his name means dove.

names.name: Amittai
names.gloss: Jonah's father, whose name is related to the Hebrew for truth or faithfulness.

names.name: Nineveh
names.gloss: A great city of Assyria on the Tigris, later its capital, near modern Mosul in Iraq.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant port in the far west, often linked with Tartessus in Spain.

names.name: Joppa
names.gloss: A port on Israel's coast, modern Jaffa beside Tel Aviv.

insights.title: Why Nineveh?
insights.body: Assyria was the empire that crushed the northern kingdom and terrorised the Near East with deliberate brutality. Nahum later celebrates Nineveh's fall. For an Israelite prophet to be sent to warn Nineveh, giving it a chance to repent, was shocking.

insights.title: Jonah in Kings
insights.body: Jonah son of Amittai appears in Kings, prophesying that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders (2 Kings 14:25). That was a message of national success. In this book he is asked to bring a message that might lead to mercy for Israel's enemy.

insights.title: Going down
insights.body: Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, and down into its innermost part (1:3, 1:5); later he will go down to the roots of the mountains (2:6). The Hebrew verb yarad is repeated deliberately. Running from God is pictured as a steady descent.

insights.title: A great storm
insights.body: The word great runs through the book: a great city, a great wind, a great storm (1:4), great fear (1:10, 1:16), a great fish (1:17). Everything around Jonah is great except his compassion. The repetition gives the story its larger-than-life feel.

insights.title: Pious pagans
insights.body: The sailors pray, try to save Jonah, and end up fearing Yahweh and offering sacrifices (1:16). Jonah, meanwhile, sleeps through the storm and confesses his faith (1:9) while running from it. The outsiders behave better than the prophet, a pattern the book repeats in Nineveh.

insights.title: Casting lots
insights.body: Casting lots (1:7) was a common ancient way of discerning the divine will. Israel used lots to divide land and to choose a goat on the Day of Atonement. The sailors' lot finds Jonah, and the book assumes God guided it.

insights.title: Take me up and throw me in
insights.body: Jonah tells the sailors to throw him overboard (1:12). Is he offering himself to save them, or does he prefer to die rather than go to Nineveh? Readers have taken it both ways. The Jewish sages also debated his motive, some suggesting he was protecting Israel.

insights.title: Three days and three nights
insights.body: The great fish was prepared by Yahweh, and Jonah was inside it three days and three nights (1:17). Jesus refers to this as the sign of Jonah, comparing it with the Son of Man's time in the heart of the earth. In Hebrew Bibles, 1:17 is counted as 2:1.

2.summary: From inside the fish, Jonah prays a psalm of thanksgiving for rescue from drowning, and Yahweh commands the fish to spit him out on dry land.
2.lookfor: Notice what Jonah thanks God for, the images of water and depth, and what is missing from his prayer.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.

insights.title: Built from the Psalms
insights.body: Jonah's prayer is full of phrases found in the Psalms: all your waves and your billows (2:3) is almost exactly Psalm 42:7. It follows the pattern of a thanksgiving psalm: distress, a cry, rescue, and a vow to sacrifice. Jonah prays in the language of Israel's worship.

insights.title: Thanksgiving before rescue
insights.body: Jonah thanks God for rescue while still inside the fish. The rescue he praises is from drowning; the fish is God's means of saving him. Some readers think the psalm looks back after the event.

insights.title: The sea and the deep
insights.body: For ancient Israelites the deep sea was a place of chaos and death, close to Sheol. Jonah describes seaweed wrapped around his head and the bars of the earth closed behind him (2:5-6). His experience is like being buried alive at the bottom of the world.

insights.title: Toward your holy temple
insights.body: Twice Jonah speaks of looking toward God's holy temple (2:4, 2:7). Even banished from God's sight, he turns toward the place where God promised to hear. Solomon had asked God to hear prayers directed toward the temple from far away.

insights.title: Lying vanities
insights.body: Jonah contrasts himself with those who regard lying vanities, idol worshippers who forsake their mercy (2:8). Yet the idol-worshipping sailors have just turned to Yahweh. Is Jonah's prayer sincere, or does it show he still has not understood God's mercy to outsiders?

insights.title: Salvation belongs to Yahweh
insights.body: The prayer ends with salvation belongs to Yahweh (2:9). That is the theme of the whole book, though Jonah will soon resent God's salvation of Nineveh. Jonah applauds mercy for himself before he objects to mercy for others.

insights.title: The fish obeys
insights.body: Yahweh speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah onto dry land (2:10). Everything in the book obeys God at once: the wind, the sea, the fish, later a plant and a worm. Only the prophet resists. The Hebrew word for fish here is dag, a general term, not specifically a whale.

insights.title: History or parable?
insights.body: Readers have long debated whether Jonah is history or a story told to teach. Jesus refers to Jonah and the Ninevites alongside the queen of Sheba, and many Christians and Jews take it as historical. Others point to its humour, exaggeration and symmetry as signs of a parable. Both groups agree on its message about God's mercy.

3.summary: Given a second chance, Jonah preaches a five-word warning in Nineveh, and the whole city, from the king to the animals, repents in sackcloth, so God relents.
3.lookfor: Notice how short Jonah's message is, how the king responds, and what God sees in 3:10.

names.name: Nineveh
names.gloss: A great Assyrian city on the Tigris.

insights.title: The second time
insights.body: Yahweh's word came to Jonah the second time (3:1), with nearly the same command as at first. This time Jonah goes. The book is a story of second chances, for the prophet as well as for Nineveh.

insights.title: Three days' journey
insights.body: Nineveh is said to be three days' journey across (3:3), much larger than any known walled city of the time. Some think the phrase includes the surrounding district or means three days to visit all its parts. Nineveh under Sennacherib had walls about twelve kilometres around.

insights.title: Five words
insights.body: Jonah's whole sermon is five words in Hebrew: In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown (3:4). It has no call to repent and no mention of God's mercy. The word overthrown, hafak, is used for Sodom, but it can also mean turned around, an irony fulfilled when Nineveh turns.

insights.title: Animals in sackcloth
insights.body: The king orders even the animals to fast and wear sackcloth (3:7-8). It sounds comic, but there are ancient reports of animals being included in mourning rituals, such as the Persians shaving their horses' manes. The scene shows the whole city's total response.

insights.title: Who knows?
insights.body: The king of Nineveh says, Who knows whether God will not turn and relent (3:9), almost the same words as Joel 2:14. A pagan king speaks like a prophet of Israel. He also names the specific sin: violence (3:8).

insights.title: God relented
insights.body: God relented (3:10) shows that the warning was conditional. Jeremiah says that if a nation God has threatened turns from evil, God will relent. Prophecy in Israel was often a call to change rather than a fixed forecast.

insights.title: The men of Nineveh
insights.body: Jesus says the men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment and condemn his generation, because they repented at Jonah's preaching (3:5), and someone greater than Jonah is here. Jews read the book of Jonah on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, as a lesson in repentance.

insights.title: Did they really repent?
insights.body: Nineveh's repentance seems sudden and total, yet Assyria remained violent, and Nahum later announces its destruction. Was the repentance real but temporary? What does the book suggest about God's response to whatever repentance is offered?

4.summary: Jonah is furious that God spared Nineveh and asks to die; God grows a plant to shade him, then destroys it, and asks Jonah whether he should not care for a great city full of people and animals.
4.lookfor: Notice why Jonah says he ran away in the first place, God's questions, and how the book ends.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: The far western port Jonah tried to flee to.

insights.title: Why Jonah ran
insights.body: Only now do we learn why Jonah fled: he knew God was gracious and merciful and would relent (4:2). His problem was not fear of failure but fear that God would forgive his enemies. The book saves the reason for the end.

insights.title: A creed turned into a complaint
insights.body: Jonah quotes God's self-description from Exodus: gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness (4:2). Joel and the Psalms use the same words in praise. Jonah uses them as an accusation.

insights.title: Better to die
insights.body: Jonah asks to die because it is better for me to die than to live (4:3, 4:8). Elijah said something similar under a broom tree. Elijah despaired at failure; Jonah despairs at success.

insights.title: Is it right to be angry?
insights.body: God answers Jonah not with argument but with a question: Is it right for you to be angry? (4:4). Jonah does not answer, but goes to watch the city. God asks again about the plant (4:9), and the book ends with a third question.

insights.title: The vine
insights.body: The plant, qiqayon in Hebrew (4:6), is often identified as the castor-oil plant, which grows fast and has large leaves. When Jerome translated it as ivy, Augustine reported that a congregation in North Africa nearly rioted because the old Latin had said gourd. The plant, worm and wind are all prepared by God, as was the fish.

insights.title: Concerned for a plant
insights.body: God's point is from lesser to greater: Jonah was concerned for a plant he did not make or tend; should God not be concerned for a city of people he made (4:10-11)? The Hebrew word means to pity or spare. Jonah's grief over the plant was really grief for his own comfort.

insights.title: And also much livestock
insights.body: The book ends with God's concern for 120,000 people who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much livestock (4:11). The last words are a surprising touch: even the animals of Nineveh matter to God. People not knowing right from left may mean children or moral ignorance.

insights.title: A question without an answer
insights.body: The book ends with God's question and no reply from Jonah. The reader is left to answer. Should God not be concerned for Nineveh? And should those who know God's mercy not want it for their enemies too?

intro.who: The book tells a story about Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet in the time of Jeroboam II, but does not say who wrote it. Jewish and Christian tradition long took it as Jonah's own account; many modern scholars see an anonymous writer from a later period telling a story with a sharp point.
intro.when: Jonah lived in the 8th century BC, when Assyria was the great power. Many scholars date the book after the exile, between the 6th and 4th centuries BC, on the basis of its language and themes; others hold to an earlier date.
intro.why: It explores God's mercy toward a violent enemy nation and a reluctant prophet, ending with a question about whether God's people will share God's compassion for outsiders.
